title: Everything a matrix can reach
objectives: Describe the column space of a matrix.
Decide whether $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has a solution by testing whether $\mathbf{b}$ is reachable.

screens.title: Hit the target
screens.prose: The matrix $\mathbf{A}$ has columns $\mathbf{a}_1 = (2, 1)$ and $\mathbf{a}_2 = (1, 2)$. The sliders set the weights $x_1$ and $x_2$. The arrows show $x_1\mathbf{a}_1$, then $x_2\mathbf{a}_2$ from its head, and their total $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$.
screens.question: Move the sliders until $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ lands on $\mathbf{b} = (4, 5)$. Which weights do it?

options.why: You swapped the weights. $2\mathbf{a}_1 + \mathbf{a}_2 = (5, 4)$, the mirror image of $\mathbf{b}$.
You copied the entries of $\mathbf{b}$ as weights. That gives $4(2, 1) + 5(1, 2) = (13, 14)$, far past $\mathbf{b}$.
That matches the first entry, $3 + 1 = 4$. The second entry is $1.5 + 2 = 3.5$, not 5.

hints.text: Start with $x_2 = 0$ and move $x_1$. Then add some $\mathbf{a}_2$ to climb towards $\mathbf{b}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the sliders to each pair and watch where $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ ends.

explain.text: One copy of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and two of $\mathbf{a}_2$, head to tail, end at $(4, 5)$. So $\mathbf{x} = (1, 2)$ solves $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$. Solving the system and building $\mathbf{b}$ from the columns are the same task.

screens.title: Parallel columns
screens.prose: A new matrix, with columns $\mathbf{a}_1 = (1, 2)$ and $\mathbf{a}_2 = (2, 4)$. The target is still $\mathbf{b} = (4, 5)$. Try to reach it.
screens.question: Can any setting of the weights reach $\mathbf{b}$?

options.text: No. Every combination lands on one line through the origin, and $\mathbf{b}$ is off it.
Yes, with weights larger than the sliders allow
options.why: Larger weights only travel further along the same line. Every combination is a multiple of $(1, 2)$, so its second entry is twice its first.

options.text: Yes, with the right mix of positive and negative weights
options.why: Negative weights point back along the same line. $(4, 5)$ is not on it, because 5 is not twice 4.

hints.text: Watch the direction of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ as you move each slider. Does it ever leave one line?

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{a}_2 = 2\mathbf{a}_1$, so both arrows point along the same line.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare $\mathbf{a}_2$ with $\mathbf{a}_1$: one is a multiple of the other.

explain.text: $\mathbf{a}_2 = 2\mathbf{a}_1$, so $x_1\mathbf{a}_1 + x_2\mathbf{a}_2 = (x_1 + 2x_2)\mathbf{a}_1$, a multiple of $(1, 2)$. Every reachable point has second entry twice its first. $(4, 5)$ fails that test, so $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has no solution.

screens.title: The column space
screens.prose: Everything $\mathbf{A}$ can reach is its **column space**, $C(\mathbf{A})$: every combination $x_1\mathbf{a}_1 + x_2\mathbf{a}_2$, with any weights. Take the matrix with columns $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 4)$ again.
screens.question: Tap every point in $C(\mathbf{A})$.

hints.text: A point is reachable when its second entry is twice its first.
Check each point against the line through $\mathbf{a}_1$: is $y = 2x$?
P: $6 = 2 \times 3$. Q: $-2 = 2 \times (-1)$. O: $0 = 2 \times 0$. R and S fail.

feedback.correct: P, Q and the origin sit on the line $y = 2x$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A point is in $C(\mathbf{A})$ when it is a multiple of $(1, 2)$.

byKey.no-origin: You left out the origin. Weights $x_1 = x_2 = 0$ reach it, so it is in every column space.
byKey.positive: You left out $Q = (-1, -2)$. Weights may be negative: $-1 \cdot \mathbf{a}_1 = (-1, -2)$.
byKey.positive-only: You kept only P. Negative weights reach Q, and zero weights reach the origin.
byKey.R: $R = (2, 1)$ has second entry half its first, not twice. It is off the line.
byKey.S: $S = (1, 3)$: 3 is not twice 1, so S is off the line.
byKey.O: You missed the origin: zero weights reach it.

explain.text: You kept P, Q and O, the points on the line $y = 2x$. That line is $C(\mathbf{A})$. The origin is always in it, since $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ gives $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$.

screens.title: Three entries, two columns
screens.prose: Now $\mathbf{A}$ is $3 \times 2$, with columns $\mathbf{a}_1 = (1, 0, 1)$ and $\mathbf{a}_2 = (0, 1, 1)$. Each $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ is a point in 3D. We list entries rather than draw them.
screens.question: Which target is in $C(\mathbf{A})$?

options.why: The first two entries force $x_1 = 2$ and $x_2 = 3$. The third is then $2 + 3 = 5$, so 6 is out of reach.
Three entries do not mean three directions. $(0, 0, 1)$ needs $x_1 = x_2 = 0$, which gives $(0, 0, 0)$.
Weights $x_1 = x_2 = 1$ match the first two entries, but give third entry $1 + 1 = 2$.

hints.text: Read $x_1$ and $x_2$ straight off the first two entries of the target.
The third entry of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ is always $x_1 + x_2$.
For $(2, 3, \cdot)$ the weights are 2 and 3, so the third entry must be 5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. In every reachable point the third entry is the sum of the first two.

explain.text: Every $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ has the form $(x_1, x_2, x_1 + x_2)$. Only $(2, 3, 5)$ passes, with $\mathbf{x} = (2, 3)$. In 3D these points fill a plane through the origin, $z = x + y$.

canvas.caption: Third entry = first + second: the plane z = x + y

screens.prose: Same $\mathbf{A}$. The target is $\mathbf{b} = (4, -1, c)$, and only $c$ is up to you.
screens.question: Which value of $c$ puts $\mathbf{b}$ in $C(\mathbf{A})$?

hints.text: The first two rows fix the weights.
Row 1 gives $x_1 = 4$ and row 2 gives $x_2 = -1$.
Row 3 then reads $c = x_1 + x_2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $x_1$ and $x_2$ from rows 1 and 2, then use row 3.

byKey.sign: You subtracted the $-1$. Row 3 adds the weights: $4 + (-1) = 3$.
byKey.any: You treated $c$ as free. Once $x_1$ and $x_2$ are fixed, row 3 fixes $c$ too.

explain.text: Rows 1 and 2 force $x_1 = 4$ and $x_2 = -1$, and row 3 then gives $c = 3$. Any other $c$ puts $\mathbf{b}$ off the plane. Two weights can fill at most a plane in 3D, never all of it.

screens.title: A square matrix
screens.prose: Now $\mathbf{A}$ is $3 \times 3$: three columns for three entries. They are $(1, 0, 1)$, $(0, 1, 1)$ and $(1, 1, 2)$.
screens.question: Can $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ be solved for $\mathbf{b} = (1, 1, 1)$?

options.text: Yes. A $3 \times 3$ matrix reaches every target in 3D.
options.why: You counted three columns and assumed three directions. Column 3 is column 1 plus column 2, so it adds no new direction.

options.text: No. Every column has third entry equal to the sum of the first two, and $\mathbf{b}$ does not.

hints.text: Compare column 3 with columns 1 and 2.
Every column satisfies $z = x + y$, so every combination does too. Does $(1, 1, 1)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a relation among the columns before trusting the shape.

byKey.square: You counted three columns and assumed three directions. Column 3 is column 1 plus column 2, so it adds no new direction.

explain.text: Column 3 equals column 1 plus column 2, so every combination still has $z = x + y$. The column space is the same plane as before. $(1, 1, 1)$ has $1 + 1 \neq 1$, so there is no solution.

screens.prose: Each time, you asked which combinations of the columns exist. $$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = x_1\mathbf{a}_1 + x_2\mathbf{a}_2 + \cdots + x_n\mathbf{a}_n$$ The **column space** $C(\mathbf{A})$ is the set of all these combinations. $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has a solution exactly when $\mathbf{b}$ is in $C(\mathbf{A})$.
screens.question: A $3 \times 2$ matrix has two columns that are not parallel. What is its column space?

options.text: A plane through the origin in 3D

options.why: Two weights move in only two directions. Filling 3D needs three directions that do not lie in one plane.
That happens only when the two columns are parallel.

options.text: A plane that may miss the origin
options.why: Weights $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ give $\mathbf{0}$, so the origin is always inside.

feedback.correct: Two independent directions span a plane, and it passes through the origin.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the directions the two columns give.

explain.text: All combinations of two non-parallel arrows fill a plane. It contains $\mathbf{0}$, from zero weights. A third entry cannot add a direction that no column has.

screens.prose: Why is $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ a combination of the columns? Take a general $2 \times 2$ matrix and expand the product.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \end{pmatrix}$, the product to expand
$= \begin{pmatrix} a x_1 + b x_2 \\ c x_1 + d x_2 \end{pmatrix}$, each row times $\mathbf{x}$
$= \begin{pmatrix} a x_1 \\ c x_1 \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} b x_2 \\ d x_2 \end{pmatrix}$, split each entry into its two terms
$= x_1\begin{pmatrix} a \\ c \end{pmatrix} + x_2\begin{pmatrix} b \\ d \end{pmatrix}$, take out the weights: a combination of the columns

hints.text: Start from the product itself.
Multiply out first, then split the result into two vectors.
The last line pulls $x_1$ and $x_2$ out as weights.

feedback.correct: Row by row, then split, then factor out the weights.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply out before you split anything.

byKey.d3: You can only split the entries once the product is multiplied out.
byKey.d4: Taking out $x_1$ and $x_2$ needs them in separate vectors first.

explain.text: Row times $\mathbf{x}$ gives $ax_1 + bx_2$ and $cx_1 + dx_2$. Splitting the terms and taking out the weights leaves $x_1(a, c) + x_2(b, d)$. The weights are the entries of $\mathbf{x}$, and the vectors are the columns.

screens.title: What can be hedged
screens.prose: A desk hedges with two instruments. The table gives each one’s exposure per contract to three risk factors, in £k per 1% move. Holding $\mathbf{x}$ contracts gives exposure $\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}$. A book is hedged exactly when $\mathbf{S}\mathbf{x}$ cancels its exposure.

state.caption: The sensitivity matrix $\mathbf{S}$: one column per instrument

screens.question: Which book exposure (equity, rates, FX), in £k, can the desk hedge exactly?

options.why: You matched the FX of the futures alone, $0.2 \times (-30)$. The swap carries FX as well, so FX must be $-6 + 2 = -4$.
Pure FX needs no equity and no rates exposure, so no contracts at all. That leaves zero FX, not 5.
You checked equity and rates only. The contracts that cancel them leave FX of 4 that nothing offsets.

hints.text: Holding $a$ futures and $b$ swaps gives exposure $(10a, 5b, 2a + b)$.
Equity and rates fix $a$ and $b$. FX is then forced.
To cancel equity $-30$ and rates $10$ you need $a = 3$ and $b = -2$. Their FX is $6 - 2 = 4$.

feedback.correct: 3 futures and $-2$ swaps give $(30, -10, 4)$, which cancels it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A book is hedgeable only if its exposure is in $C(\mathbf{S})$: FX must be $0.2 \times$ equity $+ 0.2 \times$ rates.

explain.text: Holding $a$ futures and $b$ swaps gives $(10a, 5b, 2a + b)$. To cancel $(-30, 10, -4)$ we need $a = 3$, $b = -2$, and then FX is $6 - 2 = 4$, which matches. The other books sit outside $C(\mathbf{S})$, so some risk always remains.

canvas.caption: FX exposure is forced once equity and rates are hedged

ideas: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ is a combination of the columns of $\mathbf{A}$, with the entries of $\mathbf{x}$ as weights.
The column space $C(\mathbf{A})$ holds every such combination: a line, a plane or more, always through the origin.
$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has a solution exactly when $\mathbf{b}$ is in $C(\mathbf{A})$.

formula.name: Column space
formula.note: Count the directions the columns give, not the columns.

summary.trap: A square matrix need not reach everything. A column that is a combination of the others adds no direction.

options.why: You read the ratio the wrong way round. The second entry must be three times the first.
Close, but 8 is not $3 \times 3$. Both columns have second entry three times the first.
That is the first row of $\mathbf{A}$, not a column. Columns are what get combined.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Both columns lie on the line $y = 3x$.

explain.text: $(2, 6) = 2 \cdot (1, 3)$, so $C(\mathbf{A})$ is the line $y = 3x$. Only $(3, 9)$ lies on it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve rows 1 and 2 for the weights, then use row 3.

byKey.copied: You took $x_1 = 5$ from the first entry. Row 1 is $x_1 + 2x_2 = 5$, so $x_1 = 1$.
byKey.sum: You added the first two entries of $\mathbf{b}$. Row 3 is $3x_1 + 4x_2$.

explain.text: Row 2 gives $x_2 = 2$. Row 1 gives $x_1 + 4 = 5$, so $x_1 = 1$. Row 3 then forces $c = 3 + 8 = 11$.

options.why: Each column has two entries, so every combination lives in the plane. Three columns cannot leave it.
$(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$ point in different directions, so together they reach more than a line.

feedback.correct: $(1, 0)$ and $(0, 1)$ alone reach every point of the plane.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the entries in each column first.

explain.text: Any $(p, q)$ equals $p(1, 0) + q(0, 1)$. So $C(\mathbf{A})$ is the whole plane. The third column adds nothing new, but it does no harm.

options.why: Parallel or not, adding the two inputs adds the two outputs.

options.text: Not necessarily: the sum may leave the column space
options.why: Adding two combinations of the columns gives another combination, with weights $\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try the input $\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{A}\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c}$. So the column space is closed under adding. It is closed under scaling too, which is why it is always a line, a plane or more, through the origin.
